blocks.entry_assumptions: Can read relative atomic masses from a table. Can compute with ratios and powers of ten.
blocks.inferential_jump: Particles are too small to count, but a fixed number of them (one mole, 6.022 × 10^23) always has a mass in grams equal to the relative formula mass, so weighing becomes counting.
blocks.construction: Decide which quantity you have (mass, moles or particles). Why valid: every conversion passes through moles. Convert mass to moles with n = m / M, where M is the molar mass in g/mol. Why valid: M is the mass of one mole, so dividing by it counts moles. Convert moles to particles with N = n × N_A. Why valid: each mole contains N_A particles by definition.
blocks.representation_bridge: The mole map: mass ⇄ moles ⇄ particles, with ÷M and ×N_A on the arrows; it is revealed one arrow at a time.
blocks.worked_anchor: How many molecules are in 9.0 g of water? M(H2O) = 2 × 1.0 + 16.0 = 18.0 g/mol, so n = 9.0 / 18.0 = 0.50 mol and N = 0.50 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 3.0 × 10^23 molecules.
blocks.diagnose: Does dividing grams by a pure number of particles give moles, particles, or neither?
blocks.repair: Go through moles: first divide by the molar mass, then multiply by N_A.
blocks.independent_check: Units: g ÷ (g/mol) = mol, then mol × (1/mol) = a pure count. Size: 9 g is half of 18 g, so half a mole, about 3 × 10^23 molecules.
blocks.exit_task: How many atoms of carbon are in 6.0 g of carbon (relative atomic mass 12.0)?
